summary: For ages 5–7, teach seasons and weather as a repeating annual CYCLE (spring→summer→autumn→winter→round again), anchored in observable local change: trees, clothing, daylight, activities, and weather. Hit three evidence targets — name the four seasons with typical weather, state that days are longer in summer and shorter in winter, and recognise the sequence repeats every year. Keep it strictly observational: do NOT explain WHY seasons happen (axial tilt/orbit is deferred to a later topic), and in particular avoid the 'summer is when Earth is closer to the Sun' cause-error. Observe day length by when it gets light/dark, never by looking toward the Sun. The preferred vehicle is a turnable season wheel whose coupled scene recomputes live as the child scrubs the year and loops back to spring; alternatives (paired panels, ordering/matching check, descriptive conversation, and a year-long chart) each serve distinct purposes and are preserved below.
misconceptions: 'Summer is hot because Earth is closer to the Sun.' — A very common cause-error; at this age simply avoid cause and keep to observation (mechanism is tilt/day-length, taught later).
Seasons are the same everywhere / everyone has snowy winters — seasonal weather varies by place; some regions have wet and dry seasons instead of four.
The four seasons happen in the same months worldwide — the Southern Hemisphere is opposite; at 5-7 just anchor locally and avoid overgeneralising.
Seasons are defined only by temperature — day length, plants, and animal behaviour are also part of the pattern.
The cycle has a 'start' — children may think it begins at winter/January; emphasise it's a continuous loop with no true beginning.

activities.title: Turn the season wheel: watch the year come round again
steps: Drag or turn a season wheel with your finger through the whole year.

Watch one familiar scene change in step: a bare tree pushes out blossom in spring, fills with green through the long summer days, turns gold and drops its leaves in autumn, and stands bare through the short winter days.
Watch a day-length bar swell toward summer and shrink toward winter as you turn, and notice that the tree's midday shadow on the ground is longer in winter than in summer.
Watch the little figure's clothes change from t-shirt to coat with the seasons.
Keep turning past winter until you land back in spring — the same scene you started with.
Say aloud what season comes after each one, and what happens after winter.
activities.insight: The seasons follow a fixed order that loops: after winter comes spring again. 'It repeats every year' is something you can discover by turning the wheel, not a sentence to memorise. Each season has characteristic weather AND a characteristic day length.

activities.title: Same scene, four seasons: name it and its weather
steps: Look at four panels showing the SAME scene (e.g. one tree and sky) across spring, summer, autumn and winter.
Tap each panel to reveal its season name, the typical weather for that season, and a note on day length.
Arrange the four panels in a ring to show how the sequence loops back round.
Say the four season names in order and describe one typical kind of weather for each.
activities.insight: Each season has a characteristic look and typical weather; the four together form a sequence that comes back round.

activities.title: Build a year-long weather chart
steps: Over the year, add a mark to a shared weather/temperature chart for the weather you observe locally.
Each season, compare your own trees, clothes and daylight to what you recorded.
Look back over the chart to spot the seasonal rhythm building up as real data.
Note when it gets dark across the year and compare summer with winter.
activities.insight: The seasonal pattern is something you can SEE accumulate in your own recorded observations, not just be told about. Day length is a concrete, chartable observation.

activities.title: Order and match check (after the hands-on work)
steps: Put the four seasons in order, and say what comes after autumn.
Match each season to its typical weather.
Answer: which season has the shortest days? Which has the longest?
activities.insight: A confirmation step, best used AFTER the hands-on wheel/chart work, to check whether naming, ordering, weather-matching and day-length targets have stuck. It checks the pattern but does not by itself make the child produce or explain the cycle.

activities.title: Talk about your own seasons
steps: Tell someone your favourite season and describe the weather then.
Describe each season from your own experience — what you wear, what the trees look like, when it gets dark.
Say whether where you live has four seasons, or wet and dry seasons instead.
activities.insight: Seasons are lived and local; describing them from your own experience builds and reveals the vocabulary, and shows that seasons look different in different places.

checkQuestion: It's the middle of summer, but today turned out cold and rainy. A child says, 'It must be winter now, because it's cold.' Are they right? Tell me what season it is and why.
checkAnswer: No — it's still summer. One cold, rainy day doesn't change the season. Summer is a time of year that lasts for months, and the seasons follow a fixed order that repeats every year (spring, summer, autumn, winter). A single day's weather can be different from the season's usual weather.
